cues.text: Picture two meetings.
In Marseille, two old friends kiss on both cheeks.
In Chicago, two people meet and choose a handshake or a hug.
Earlier, we saw that the relationship chooses the greeting.
Here, we look at what happens when the greeting is missing, and at how body space works.
A cheek kiss is an informal greeting.
It can show friendship, family ties, respect or comfort.
So in places where cheek kissing is normal, the kiss carries a message.
If you do not kiss, people may read a message too.
They can feel dislike or offense.
France is not the same everywhere.
The number of kisses changes from region to region.
There is even a French joke: you can know which city you are in by counting the kisses.
In southern France, even two men often greet with cheek kisses.
In northern France, this happens less.
So "the French kiss" is really many local habits.
What about handshakes and hugs?
In some English-speaking countries, such as Australia and New Zealand, cheek kisses happen only among close friends, and handshakes or hugs are more common greetings.
A handshake or a hug can do the same job as a kiss: it says how close two people are, but with a different kind of touch.
Body space also has rules.
Scientists who study space between people describe four zones: intimate, personal, social and public.
We let a person into a closer zone when we feel closer to them.
Americans like about the same personal space as people in northern and central Europe.
In Japan, everyday greetings usually have less touching, so kisses, hugs and handshakes are less common than in many other places.
So a greeting is like a ruler.
It measures the relationship, and each culture marks the lines in a slightly different place.
In France, you enter a bakery and say, "A baguette, please."
The baker looks less friendly than before.
What went wrong?
You forgot one word: Bonjour.
Saying Bonjour before any request is a basic rule of politeness in shops, cafés and bakeries.
It helps you avoid a cold welcome.
People appreciate it even if it is the only French word you know.
The word comes first because it treats the worker as a person first and a service second.
The French words tu and vous do a similar job.
Both mean "you."
Tu is close and informal.
Vous shows respect or social distance.
Many languages have a choice like this.
In the past, French speakers often used tu and vous in the same situations.
Over time, clearer patterns grew.
English you is different.
It is less formal than vous, and it does not push people apart.
This matters for visitors.
When a French person uses vous with you, it is not coldness.
It is respect.
Distance at the start is a polite way to say, "I take you seriously."
In a line at an American supermarket, a stranger says, "Cold today, huh?"
You may never see this person again.
So why talk at all?
Small talk opens a conversation.
It shows strangers that you have friendly plans, not bad ones.
It also keeps social bonds alive and helps people manage the distance between them.
Small talk works at the end of a talk too.
A few light words like "Have a good day!"
make leaving softer, so it does not feel like rejection.
So small talk is a tool for the edges of a relationship.
It lets two strangers be warm for one minute and then leave without any problem.
This is why some visitors misunderstand Americans.
They hear friendly words and expect a deep friendship.
But the friendly words are often a polite way to share a small, safe space.
Compare this with France.
French politeness puts the respectful word, Bonjour, at the door.
American politeness often puts a light chat there.
Both are careful ways to handle a stranger.
An American visitor in Paris leaves a big tip that nobody expected.
A French visitor in New York leaves no tip, and the server is upset.
Both made the same mistake from opposite sides.
History helps explain this.
In 1919, Prohibition put money pressure on restaurants in the USA.
So they accepted tips to add to their workers' pay.
In this way, the tip slowly became part of the wage, not only a small extra "thank you."
That is why many American workers depend on tips.
But the system has problems.
Tipping can feel awkward, because people are not sure how much to give.
It is also not always fair.
People sometimes tip by the price of the meal, not by the quality of the service.
And the system is hard to change.
Some people argue that changing the tip rules could favor servers who get tips over staff who do not get tips, and make income less equal.
So in the USA, a tip is not a gift you can easily skip.
It is part of how workers get paid.
At lunchtime in Paris, office workers leave their desks to eat.
In many American towns, lunch may be a quick burger.
Is one way better?
It is more useful to ask what each meal protects.
In France, enjoying food is an important value.
In the 20th century, Georges Auguste Escoffier wrote down the rules of high French cooking.
Today, a lunch break usually lasts at least one hour.
Eating lunch at your desk is even illegal.
But a long lunch does not mean a big meal.
On busy workdays in Paris, lunches with many courses are not common.
French food has also changed.
Many modern meals are simpler, and some dishes come from immigrant cooking.
Fast food and new habits among young people put pressure on the old food culture.
Even so, France works to keep it, for example through education programs in schools.
American food grew from a different story.
US culture was shaped by history, geography and immigration.
Famous foods like apple pie and hamburgers come from immigrant and local roots.
Fast food is a common part of American meals, and people worry that it adds calories and leads to health problems.
So the French lunch protects time to enjoy food with others.
The quick American meal reflects a mixed food story and a busy day.
